title: Chirurgie des surfaces conformes : notes manuscrites (s.d., 1983-1984), lettres (1984).

deep.reconstruction:
Context: Grothendieck is classifying real elliptic curves, which are the 'conformal tori' of genus 1 with an antiholomorphic involution. A real elliptic curve gives a lattice π ≅ Z² with an involution σ induced by complex conjugation. The previous page treats the two families E_a (τ = √a·i) and E'_a (τ = ½(1+√a·i)). This page abstracts the lattice-with-involution problem over a base ring h.

Hypotheses: 2 is a non-zero-divisor in h ('2-régulier'), and k_0 = h/2h is a field.

Corollary 1. Let M be free of rank 2 with an involution σ ≠ ±1. Put P = M_+ = ker(σ−1) and Q = M_− = ker(σ+1), each free of rank 1.
- Since 2x = (x+σx) + (x−σx), we have 2M ⊂ P⊕Q ⊂ M.
- So M/(P⊕Q) embeds in (½P⊕½Q)/(P⊕Q) ≅ P/2P ⊕ Q/2Q.
- Since M∩½P = P and M∩½Q = Q, the image u is a k_0-subspace meeting both coordinate lines trivially.
- Hence u = 0, or u is the graph of an isomorphism P/2P → Q/2Q.
This gives an equivalence (M,σ) ↔ (P, Q, u).

Corollary 2. Suppose h* → k_0* is surjective, so bases of P/2P and Q/2Q lift to bases of P and Q. Then the conjugacy classes in GL(2,h) of elements of exact order 2 (≠ ±1) are exactly two:
- diag(1,−1), the case u = 0;
- the 'glued' class, case u = diagonal.

Model of the glued class: P = Q = h and M' = (2h⊕2h) + diag(h⊕h) = {(x,y) | x−y ∈ 2h}, with σ(x,y) = (x,−y). Take the basis e_0 = (2,0), e_1 = (1,1). Then σe_0 = e_0 and σe_1 = (1,−1) = e_0 − e_1, so the matrix of σ is [[1,1],[0,−1]]. The bottom margin checks σ² = 1.

For h = Z this is the reflection of the hexagonal lattice A_2 in the axis through a vertex, written in oblique coordinates on two consecutive vertices (z ↦ z̄ sends ω = e^{iπ/3} to 1−ω).

NB on the real picture. Over R, with u_± spanning Π_±, σ_R = diag(1,−1) in both cases. The lattice is:
- Zu_+ + Zu_− (rectangular) in the first case;
- {x u_+ + y u_− : x, y ∈ ½Z, x−y ∈ Z} (rhombic, centred) in the second.
These match E_a and E'_a. The next page uses this to count real components (2 versus 1) and to compute H¹(Gal, E) for torsors.
errors: Minor: the identification of M/(P⊕Q) with u also tacitly needs P and Q free of rank 1 (true over a PID or local ring). Without the hypothesis h*→k_0* surjective, the second family splits into classes indexed by k_0*/im(h*), as Grothendieck himself notes in a struck-out line.

Notational clash: 'u' denotes both the subspace of P/2P⊕Q/2Q and a lattice vector in the hexagon discussion. No mathematical error found; the computations σe_1 = e_0 − e_1, the matrix, and σ² = 1 are correct.

ideas.what: Classification of involutions of a rank-2 lattice via the eigenlattices M_+, M_- and a gluing subspace in M_+/2M_+ ⊕ M_-/2M_-
ideas.modern_name: Gluing of primitive eigensublattices along discriminant groups; integral representations of C_2
ideas.usually_credited_to: Diederichsen (1940) and Reiner (1957) for Z[C_p]-lattices; Nikulin (1979) for gluing formalism

ideas.what: Two conjugacy classes of non-central involutions in GL(2,Z): diag(1,-1) and [[1,1],[0,-1]] (regular representation Z[C_2])
ideas.modern_name: Classification of involutions in GL_2(Z); rectangular vs rhombic real lattices
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical (Klein; for real elliptic curves Alling 1981, Silhol 1982)

ideas.what: Realisation of the glued class as reflection of the hexagonal lattice in a vertex axis
ideas.modern_name: Reflection in the A_2 lattice / Weyl group element

deep.surprise_reason: A careful but standard working-out of the classification of real lattices (equivalently, rank-2 Z[C_2]-lattices) used to classify real elliptic curves. The slight generalisation to rings with h/2h a field is routine and well known in integral representation theory.
transcription_corrections: 'P_{2p}⊗Q_{2q}' is better read as P/2P ⊕ Q/2Q (quotients mod 2), not a tensor product.
In 'Celles correspondant à', read 'P = h, Q = h' and 'M' = (2h⊕2h) + diag de h⊕h', not 'k'.
The inserted '{+𝔆 est des+}' is likely '(M,σ) précédents' with the insertion '2-régulier' attached to the hypothesis (possibly 'anneau' rather than 'groupe').
The margin note 'u=2e0, v=...' is uncertain. Given the next page (σu = u, σv = u − v), it more likely identifies u, v with e_0, e_1 up to scaling.
'Dans le cas où h = Z' is correct; the hexagon has vertices e_0 = u_+, e_1, e_1 − e_0, −e_0, −e_1, e_0 − e_1 = σe_1.
